variants.text: Cowra is a town of about 8,000 people on the Lachlan River, around 310 km west of Sydney. During the Second World War it held a prisoner-of-war camp, and on 5 August 1944 more than a thousand Japanese prisoners broke out; the sites left from that night, and the Japanese war cemetery beside the town, are why many visitors come. The town's response was a Japanese garden, designed by Ken Nakajima as a strolling garden to symbolise reconciliation and peace. Cowra is also the base for a wine region of 40-plus vineyards around Cowra, Billimari and Canowindra.
variants.claims: ~8,250 people (Wikipedia; 'about 8,000' per unverified note), Lachlan River, ~310 km west of Sydney, POW camp, Breakout date and 1,104 POWs (Wikipedia Cowra, Wikipedia Cowra breakout); Nakajima, kaiyu-shiki strolling garden, reconciliation and peace (cowragarden.com.au); 40+ vineyards around Cowra, Billimari and Canowindra (Wikivoyage Cowra). Caveat: 'The town's response was a Japanese garden' is an inference linking garden to Breakout; research only says the garden symbolises reconciliation after WWII. Use variant 2 if that link is not wanted.

variants.text: Cowra sits on the Lachlan River in the Central West, 310 km west of Sydney and 189 km north of Canberra, where three highways meet. It is best known for two things from the Second World War: the 1944 prisoner-of-war breakout, and the Japanese garden and cemetery that now stand for peace between the two countries. The Japanese war cemetery on Doncaster Drive is the only one in Australia. Beyond the town, 40-plus vineyards around Cowra, Billimari and Canowindra make it a wine base, and Canowindra lies 32 km north.
variants.claims: Central West, 310 km west of Sydney, 189 km north of Canberra, junction of Mid-Western, Olympic highways and Lachlan Valley Way (Wikipedia Cowra, Wikivoyage Cowra); garden symbolises reconciliation and peace after WWII (cowragarden.com.au); only Japanese war cemetery in Australia, Doncaster Drive (Wikivoyage Cowra); 40+ vineyards (Wikivoyage Cowra); Canowindra 32 km north (Wikipedia Canowindra).

variants.text: Cowra is a Lachlan River town of around 8,000 where the Mid-Western Highway, Olympic Highway and Lachlan Valley Way meet. It was the site of a Second World War prisoner-of-war camp, and the breakout of 5 August 1944 is the largest prison escape of the war. Visitors walk the camp site, visit the Japanese and Australian war cemeteries side by side, and stroll the 12.5-acre Japanese garden. Spring brings cherry blossom to the garden and April brings balloons to Canowindra, 32 km north.
variants.claims: Highways junction, population (Wikipedia Cowra); 5 Aug 1944, largest prison escape of WWII (Wikipedia Cowra breakout); Australian cemetery beside Japanese cemetery (Wikivoyage Cowra); 12.5 acres (cowragarden.com.au, operator claim); cherry blossom spring (cowragarden.com.au, sakura_matsuri); April Balloon Challenge (Wikipedia Canowindra, canowindrachallenge.org.au). Caveat: 'spring brings cherry blossom' rests on a web-search summary of the blossom window (late Sep to mid Oct), flagged unverified in research.

highlights.note: One per reason, 2-3 words, same order.
highlights.claims: Strolling garden/kaiyu-shiki/cultural centre: cowragarden.com.au; Sakura Avenue and camp site: Wikivoyage Cowra; Japanese war cemetery: Wikivoyage Cowra; fossils, historic town, balloons: Wikipedia Canowindra.

tips: The Japanese Garden costs $22 for adults ($17 concession or local, $12 child, $52 family) and opens 8:30 am to 5 pm daily; prices differ on festival days.
Plan to drive: public transport is two NSW TrainLink coach services a day from Bathurst or Lithgow, there is no airport in town, and Canowindra is reached by car.
Book early for festival weekends, the Sakura Matsuri in late September and the Canowindra Balloon Challenge in April.
variants.claims: Prices and hours: cowragarden.com.au; coach only, no airport (Wikivoyage Cowra, timetable dated so no times given); festivals: cowragarden.com.au/about-1, ageoffishes.org.au. Garden prices are as at research date and not independently dated.

tips: The garden is not flat, so mobility can be a factor, and dogs on a lead are welcome except during the Sakura Matsuri.
Scheduled flights serve Orange, Parkes and Bathurst, not Cowra, and it is about 1.5 hours' drive from Bathurst or Orange.
If you add Canowindra's Age of Fishes Museum, note it is closed Tuesday and Wednesday outside NSW school holidays.
variants.claims: Mobility and dogs: cowragarden.com.au; nearest scheduled flights Orange, Parkes, Bathurst and ~1.5 h drive (Wikivoyage Cowra); museum closure (ageoffishes.org.au). The third tip is valid only if the Age of Fishes Museum is added to the app; otherwise drop it.
